extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; poets, dramatists, and critics studying classical poetics and principles of poetic/dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle-derived principles for composing and evaluating poetry and drama (especially Greek/classical models), focusing on unity, universality, characterisation, and the balance between fancy and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: “action by degrees gains strength and consistency, till, like that of tragedy, it has a beginning, a middle, and an end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should form a coherent whole with a clear beginning, middle and end; scenes and incidents must be organized so action increases in strength and consistency rather than remaining a loose sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and action intimately united
rubrics_metrics.description: “Character and action become more intimately united.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' traits should be organically related to the events they drive and to the plot's development; action should reveal character and vice versa, not be mere stage dressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral probability / internal plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “moral probability takes the place of the arbitrary sequence of loosely connected scenes and incidents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events should follow from moral/psychological plausibility and internal logic rather than arbitrary contrivance; actions must seem likely given characters' motives and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy generalises characters (typification)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the characters in comedy are ‘general’… Comedy … is to embody a dominant characteristic or a leading passion, so that the single attribute becomes the man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often abstracts and amplifies a single trait to create a type or personified ideal; this generalisation is a legitimate method but risks caricature if overdone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy focuses on single aspects and limits scope
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy looking at a single aspect of life… withdraws its attention from the graver issues which concern the end of conduct. ... it cannot, while remaining within its own strict limits, present, as tragedy does, a rounded and complete action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the narrower moral/ethical ambition of comedy: fine for exposing follies and limitations but not for delivering the rounded, universal action of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of comic abstraction toward caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: “A character so created, exhibiting an ideal of covetousness, misanthropy, or whatever the quality may be, almost of necessity runs to caricature. It is framed on lines of impossible simplicity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When isolating a dominant trait, avoid impossible simplicity; maintain organic connections to other impulses to prevent flat caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy unites the individual and the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: “Greek tragedy... combines in one harmonious representation the individual and the universal. Whereas comedy tends to merge the individual in the type, tragedy manifests the type through the individual.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for characters who are true persons (complex, contradictory) yet reveal universal human truths; tragedy should present the particular as expressive of the general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounded and complete action in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “[tragedy] present[s] ... a rounded and complete action, an image of universal human nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic plot should strive for completeness and unity that conveys universal human meaning—more than episodic or merely satirical incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as mediator between comedy and tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humour is the meeting-point of tragedy and comedy… Humour, enriched by sympathy, directs its observation to the more serious realities of life. ... pathos henceforth becomes the companion of humour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour with sympathy to probe deeper contradictions and mixed emotions; enriched humour can generalise while preserving individuality and moral depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even fantastic licence must have intelligible drift/purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fantastic license, however, of comedy stands alone in Greek literature. In other departments fancy is much more restrained… Yet even comedy has its lucid intervals, or rather in its madness there is a method. In its wildest freaks there is some underlying reason, some intelligible drift and purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wild invention or fantasy is acceptable only when governed by a discernible purpose or underlying structure that serves the work's overall meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure realism (literal imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “First, pure realism is forbidden; that is, the literal and prosaic imitation which reaches perfection in a jugglery of the senses by which the copy is mistaken for the original.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should not simply copy surface detail for its own sake; poetic representation should shape and select reality toward intelligible, harmonious expression rather than sensory trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure symbolism (fantastic hybrids)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Next, pure symbolism is forbidden,—those fantastic shapes … which in transcending nature violates nature's laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute implausible symbol-machinery (hybrid monsters, meaningless allegory) for believable imaginative representation; symbolic elements must cohere with poetic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth: making the impossible plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: “The irrational elements (τὰ ἄλογα) being but accessories that do not disturb the main impression. They are presented to the imagination with such vividness and coherence that the impossible becomes plausible, the fiction looks like truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural or implausible material may be used provided it is presented with internal coherence and vividness that preserve the work's plausibility and emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control by reason, measure and self-restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Greek imagination of the classical age is under the strict control of reason, it is limited by a sense of measure and a faculty of self-restraint. ... We are always conscious of a reserve of power, a temperate strength which knows its own resources and employs them without effort and without ostentation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and balance in imaginative expression; do not dazzle gratuitously—seek harmonious, measured expression rather than excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration tempered by artistic law
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Greeks themselves were accustomed to speak of poetic genius as a form of madness… Even Aristotle, who sometimes writes as if the faculty of the logician were enough to construct a poem, says ‘poetry is a thing inspired.’ … they never released themselves from the sovereignty of reason. Capricious and inconsequent they were not.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow inspired or ecstatic creativity but ensure it is disciplined and conforms to artistic principles—poetic ecstasy must still obey an underlying order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at the universal (poetic universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the effort of poetry is towards the universal; that it represents the permanent possibilities of human nature, the essentials rather than the accidents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful poem or drama reveals enduring human possibilities and truths rather than merely recording accidental, idiosyncratic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic sequence should be logical/necessary, not merely empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sequence of poetry is not the empirical sequence of fact but the logical or conceivable sequence of ideas; it eliminates chance and discovers unity and significance in characters and events.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange events according to intelligible causal and thematic necessity so the work uncovers meaning and unity rather than a random chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify particulars only insofar as they serve the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: “The vulgar and obtrusive elements of personality are cast off, and in proportion as the characters are divested of what is purely individual, do they gain in interest and elevation. … In discarding what is accidental their individuality is not obliterated but deepened and enriched; for it is not disordered emotion or perplexity of motive that makes a character poetical, but power of will or power of love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit or downplay accidental, distracting details that do not contribute to the work's essential insight; retain or deepen traits that serve the character's universal significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit detail only if contributing to the total impression and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The finer shades of character are not excluded by the simplicity with which the main lines are drawn. In discarding what is accidental their individuality is not obliterated but deepened and enriched; … the utmost variety of detail is admitted, if only it contributes to the total impression and is subject to a controlling unity of design.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow variety and subtle detail, but ensure each detail supports the overall unity and total impression; stray particulars that distract from unity should be excised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as concrete philosophy (express universal via sensuous form)
rubrics_metrics.description: “poetry is akin to philosophy in so far as it aims at expressing the universal; but that, unlike philosophy, it employs the medium of sensuous and Imaginative form, In this sense poetry is a concrete philosophy, ‘a criticism of life’ and of the universe.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to embody a consistent, harmonious wisdom about life in sensuous imaginative terms rather than abstract argument; the poem's form should enact its insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth/history to give perspective and universality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Myth was the unwritten literature of an early people, whose instinctive language was poetry… Myth was the golden link which bound together the generations. … The ode rises by clear ascents from the individual to the universal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ mythic or historic materials to lift particular events into larger, communal or universal contexts; myth can transfigure the present into enduring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal elements (e.g., metre) are subordinate to poetic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “He holds that metre, which was popularly thought to be the most essential element of poetry, is in truth the least essential, if indeed it is essential at all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let formal technicalities (strict metre, ornament) dominate at the expense of universality, plausibility, or the work's inner unity; form should serve substance.
